title: Cold-start Warmup Orchestration Runbook
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:
This runbook defines the operational procedures, automated orchestration patterns, and diagnostics used to mitigate cold-start latency for model-serving pods (hosted and dedicated) across Redwood’s platform. It covers proactive warmup, on-demand prefetch, health checks, rollout strategies, dashboarding, and post-incident review steps.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce user-perceived latency spikes caused by cold starts (model loading, kernel JIT, allocator ramp-up, cache misses) while balancing cost and GPU pool utilization.
- Scope: Applies to inference services managed by the serving runtime (all model families), relevant autoscaling controllers, and prefix/KV cache infrastructure for hosted and dedicated clusters. Does NOT cover user application cold-starts (frontend or upstream proxies).

Owners and contacts:
- Runbook owner: eng-platform - Model Serving Reliability (oncall contact: lucas.chen@redwood.com)
- Primary implementer: eng-serving-runtime (lead: Morgan Reyes)
- Cross-team reviewers: eng-sre, eng-infra, customer-success (for enterprise-private configurations)
- Pager escalation: follow standard platform escalation ladder; page eng-sre when SLA degradation persists > 15m.

Key metrics and SLO impact:
- Primary SLOs affected: p95 inference latency (default SLO target: 250ms for small models, 800ms for large models), error rate, and request queue depth.
- Early-warning metrics: sudden increase in pod restart-rate (>2x baseline over 10m), model-load time > configured threshold (default 30s), cache miss rate spike > 30% relative increase, GPU memory pressure > 85%.
- Cost tradeoff: pre-warming increases reserved GPU hours; target objective is to keep p95 latency within SLO while limiting dedicated idle GPU time to <8% of pool capacity in steady-state.

Definitions and failure modes:
- Cold-start: any request that causes the service to pay a non-trivial startup cost (model load, kernel compilation, JIT warmup, allocator growth).
- Warmup: deterministic sequence of lightweight inference requests that initialize kernels, populate prefix/KV caches, and stabilize memory allocators.
- Failure modes:
  1) Slow cold-loads: model artifacts fetched from object store are slow (S3 latency).
  2) JIT/compilation stall: first N tokens trigger heavy kernel compilation causing tail latency.
  3) Memory pressure evictions: pods OOM or are OOM-killed during concurrent warmups.
  4) Cache churn: warmup requests evict hot prefixes when run at scale causing subsequent real requests to hit misses.

Preconditions and safety checks (automated):
1) Verify model artifact checksum and existence in model-catalog (API: GET /models/{model_id}/artifact).
2) Ensure node has GPU memory headroom > 10% before warmup triggers.
3) Throttle concurrent warmup jobs per-gpu (default: 4 per A100-40GB equivalent).
4) Confirm storage bandwidth (s3/get throughput) within expected SLA.
5) Validate warmup image/container matches runtime version (label: runtime_version).

Automated orchestration patterns (recommended):
- Predictive warmup at scale:
  1) Trigger: scheduled window before expected traffic spike (regional traffic forecast).
  2) Mechanism: controller creates WarmupJob resources (K8s CRD) that allocate minimal pods with init-container performing artifact fetch and health-checks.
  3) Warmup sequence: small batch of zero-shot prompts that touch common attention patterns and typical sequence lengths.
  4) Completion criteria: model-load-time < configured target (default 8s) AND kv-cache hit-rate > 60% on synthetic probe.
- Reactive on-demand warming:
  1) Trigger: first request queueing > queue_threshold_ms (default 100ms) OR model-cache-miss-rate spike.
  2) Mechanism: controller spins up pre-warm pods in fast-path (use burst credits) and routes a configurable sample of traffic to them for warmup probing.
- Canary-aware warmup during rollouts:
  1) New model versions receive a staged warmup: small canary warmup, traffic sample, measure quality and latency, then scale to full warmup.
  2) If p95 grows > 20% during canary, abort rollout and scale down warmup jobs.

Warmup job design (implementation notes):
- WarmupPod lifecycle:
  - Init: pull model artifact, unpack to local NVMe, run model integrity check (sha256).
  - Probe: run 3 fast inference probes across seq-lengths [8, 64, 256] and record kernel compile durations and memory high-water mark.
  - Prefetch: optionally pre-populate KV-prefix cache for top-100 prefixes for customer workloads (configurable per-customer or per-tenant).
  - Mark ready: report to placement controller only after probes pass thresholds.
- Sample warmup probe payloads (JSON):
  {"prompt":"<warmup-short>","max_tokens":8}
  {"prompt":"<warmup-mid>","max_tokens":64}
  {"prompt":"<warmup-long>","max_tokens":256}

Safe throttles and knobs:
- warmup.concurrent_limit_per_gpu: integer (default 4)
- warmup.max_reserved_seconds: integer (default 900) - max wallclock seconds a warm pod can stay idle before release
- warmup.prefetch_prefix_count: integer (default 100)
- warmup.backpressure_threshold: queue_ms (default 200)
- warmup.safety_memory_headroom_pct: integer (default 10)

Operational runbook steps (when customers report cold-start spikes):
1) Triage: gather scope (region, model_id, deployment_type, time window). Query platform dashboard for pod restarts, model-load time histogram, and warmup job activity.
2) Quick mitigation (<= 15min):
   - If model-load times are high: manually launch a WarmupJob against affected model instances in the region (CLI: redwoodctl warmup create --model MODEL_ID --region us-west-2 --count 2 --prefetch-prefixes 100).
   - If GPU memory pressure: reduce concurrent warmups (redwoodctl warmup set-concurrency --model MODEL_ID --value 1) and scale down non-critical pools.
   - If S3 latency: use cached artifact mirror (fallback: pull from regional mirror endpoint) and contact eng-infra for upstream S3 health.
3) Monitor: observe p95, kernel_compile_time, and kv_cache_hit_rate. If metrics improve to within SLO, schedule automated warmup policy for off-peak hours.
4) Escalation: if manual warmup does not restore SLO within 30m, page eng-sre and consider draining and rescheduling affected nodes (possible underlying hardware flakiness).

Diagnostics and queries (use these dashboards/queries):
- Dashboards: "Model Load & Warmup" (panel: model_load_time histogram, kernel_compile_time heatmap, kv_cache_hit_rate), "Warmup Job Fleet" (active jobs, queued jobs, per-gpu concurrency).
- PromQL examples:
  - model_load_time_seconds_bucket{job="model-loader",model_id=~"$MODEL"}
  - histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_compile_time_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_id))
  - sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total[5m])) by (model_id, region)
- Logs: search for init-container stderr related to artifact fetch and unpack errors. Common error keywords: "tar: unexpected EOF", "checksum mismatch", "OutOfMemoryError", "cuBLAS init failed".

Dashboarding and alerts (config recommendations):
- Create alert when: model_load_time_95th > 30s for 5m -> severity P1 (page oncall).
- Alert: kernel_compile_time_95th > 5s -> severity P2, notify eng-serving-runtime slack channel.
- Alert: warmup_concurrent_limit_exhausted -> severity P3, notify eng-platform-runbooks channel.
- Dashboard panels to include: per-model load time, warmup job lag, per-node GPU headroom, KV cache hit/miss ratios, request queue depth.

Rollout and policy guidance:
- For new model families: enable scheduled predictive warmup for first 72 hours of production traffic; collect compile profiles to build kernel cache artifacts.
- For enterprise/private deployments: prefer manual warmup orchestration with customer approval to avoid cross-tenant prefetch. Document per-customer prefetch allowlist.
- Cost control: cap total warmup reserved-GPU hours by tenant and pool. Include warmup usage in monthly chargeback reporting for Dedicated customers.

Post-incident review checklist (retrospective steps):
1) Record timeline: discovery -> mitigations -> resolution -> verification.
2) Root cause classification: network artifact fetch vs runtime compilation vs autoscaler behavior.
3) Action items: config changes, prefetch allowlists, S3 mirror setup, kernel-cache bake tasks. Assign owners and target completion dates.
4) Metrics to track post-change: reduction in model_load_time_95th, warmup-job wall time, and reserved-GPU time fraction.

Runbook automation examples (CLI snippets):
- Create a predictive warmup job:
  redwoodctl warmup create --model gptx-12b-v2 --region eu-west-1 --schedule "2026-03-01T03:00:00Z" --concurrency 3 --prefetch 100
- Query warmup job status:
  redwoodctl warmup list --model gptx-12b-v2 --region eu-west-1 --output table
- Adjust concurrency on the fly:
  redwoodctl warmup set-concurrency --job JOB_ID --value 1

Backout and rollback procedures:
- Immediate backout: reduce or cancel warmup jobs and scale down reserved nodes. If warmup caused memory churn, restart affected pods after reducing concurrency.
- If warmup probe reveals corrupted artifact: mark model version as quarantined in model-catalog and trigger automated rollback to previous stable model version.

Known limitations and risks:
- Large-scale prefetch can cause unintended cache eviction for other hot models; use prefix budgets and per-tenant allowlisting.
- Warmup increases temporary storage and network I/O; abuse could overload artifact storage if not rate-limited.
- Kernel compilation heterogeneity across hardware families may require separate warmup probe profiles per instance type.

Implementation roadmap (short-term tactical -> long-term vision):
- Q1 (tactical): add WarmupJob CRD, implement throttles and CLI, basic dashboard panels.
- Q2 (stabilize): integrate warmup telemetry into rollout pipelines, add per-tenant prefetch allowlist, cost accounting.
- Q3 (optimization): kernel cache artifact baking and regional artifact mirrors to remove S3 tail latencies.

Appendix: quick checklist for oncall responders
- Check model-load-time panel for affected model_id.
- If model_load_time_95th > 30s: run manual warmup job x2.
- If GPU memory pressure: lower warmup concurrency and restart warmup pods.
- If S3 errors: failover to regional mirror and page storage team.
- Document incident in postmortem tracker and assign action items.
